slides.title: Defining a Class
slides.content: A class groups related data and behavior. Use the class keyword followed by a name and braces.
slides.exampleOutput: Class definition with a method that writes to the console; produces no output unless the method is invoked.

exercise.prompt: Which keyword defines a class in C#?

slides.title: Creating Objects
slides.content: Use the new keyword to create an instance of a class. The object holds its own copy of instance fields.
slides.exampleOutput: Declaration or expression only; produces no console output.

exercise.prompt: Create a Dog object named dog: Dog dog = new _____();

slides.title: Accessing Members
slides.content: Use the dot operator to access fields and methods on an object instance.

exercise.prompt: Drag the correct operator to call a method: myCar [ ? ] Drive();

slides.title: Multiple Objects
slides.content: You can create many objects from one class. Each object is independent and has its own state.
slides.exampleOutput: Declaration or expression only; produces no console output.

exercise.prompt: Create two Person objects and set their Name fields to different values.
hints: Make sure your code includes the required keywords/elements: new Person()
When run, your code should output: Compiles with two Person instances.

slides.title: Constructors
slides.content: Constructors run when an object is created. They initialize state and have the same name as the class.
slides.exampleOutput: Class definition; produces no console output.

exercise.prompt: What is special about a constructor name?
options: It must match the class name
exercise.answer: It must match the class name

slides.title: Default Constructor
slides.content: If no constructor is defined, C# provides a parameterless default constructor that initializes fields to default values.
slides.example:
class Book { public string Title; }
Book b = new Book(); // default constructor
slides.exampleOutput: Class definition; produces no console output.

exercise.prompt: C# supplies a parameterless constructor if you define _____ constructors.

slides.title: Object References
slides.content: Class variables store references, not the object itself. Assigning one variable to another copies the reference.
slides.example:
Car a = new Car();
Car b = a; // both refer to same Car
slides.exampleOutput: Declaration or expression only; produces no console output.

exercise.prompt: Drag what Car variables store: Car c = new Car(); [?]

slides.title: Classes Review
slides.content: Classes define object blueprints. Use constructors to initialize objects and access members with the dot operator.

exercise.prompt: Define a class Laptop with a constructor that takes a string brand and stores it in a field Brand.
hints: Make sure your code includes the required keywords/elements: class, Laptop, Brand
When run, your code should output: Brand, Brand
